summary: Lets an IMAP client send its initial authentication data along with the AUTHENTICATE command, instead of waiting for the server to ask for it. This saves one round trip at the start of a session, which matters on slow or high-latency networks. It is a standards-track IMAP extension.

eli5.summary: Instead of knocking and waiting to be asked who you are, you say your name as you knock, which saves a back-and-forth.

subtitle: Lets an IMAP client send its first SASL authentication data with the AUTHENTICATE command, saving a round trip.

tldr.problem: IMAP's SASL profile always needed at least one full round trip to authenticate because the AUTHENTICATE command could not carry an initial client response. That delay hurts when round-trip costs are high.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds an optional second argument to AUTHENTICATE holding the base64-encoded initial response, and servers advertise support with the SASL-IR capability.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers that support it can skip a round trip at the start of a session. Support is optional on both sides, and the old exchange still works.

today: RFC 4959 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
Until now, IMAP's use of SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) never supported an initial client response, so every authentication needed at least one complete round trip. The RFC calls this extra round trip at the start of a session undesirable, especially when round-trip costs are high.

A server supports this extension if it lists SASL-IR in its CAPABILITY response. Such a server accepts an optional initial client response on the AUTHENTICATE command for any SASL mechanism that supports one, as defined in RFC 4422.
sections.eli5: It is like telling the receptionist your name while you walk in, instead of waiting for them to ask.

sections.title: The Changed AUTHENTICATE Command
sections.content:
The extension adds an optional second argument to the AUTHENTICATE command from RFC 3501. That argument carries the initial client response from RFC 4422.

The response MUST be encoded as in RFC 4648 (base64), and MUST be sent outside of a quoted string or literal. To send a zero-length initial response, the client MUST send a single pad character, =, which means a response is present but empty.

Servers decode errors just as IMAP handles any normal SASL client response. They should reject characters outside the base64 alphabet and any pad character that is not at the end, so =AAA and AAA=BBB are not allowed. If a client sends an initial response with a mechanism that does not support one, the server MUST reject the command with a tagged BAD.

The formal syntax is authenticate = "AUTHENTICATE" SP auth-type [SP (base64 / "=")] *(CRLF base64), and SASL-IR is added to the capability rule.
sections.eli5: You put your secret answer on the same line as your request, written in a special code. If you have nothing to say, you write a single equals sign to mean "I answered, but it is empty."

sections.title: Optional Use and Fallback
sections.content:
Using the initial response is optional for both clients and servers. A server that implements the extension MUST still support clients that leave it out. A client that implements it MUST NOT send an initial response to a server that does not advertise SASL-IR, and MUST fall back to the compatible mode of RFC 3501.

When either side lacks the capability, a mechanism that uses an initial client response is negotiated with the ordinary challenge/response exchange, starting with a zero-length server challenge.
sections.eli5: If the other side does not understand the shortcut, you use the old, longer way. Nothing breaks.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows the PLAIN mechanism over TLS. After the server lists SASL-IR and AUTH=PLAIN, the client sends A01 AUTHENTICATE PLAIN dGVzdAB0ZXN0AHRlc3Q= and the server replies A01 OK Success (tls protection) at once. Without the initial response the client sends AUTHENTICATE PLAIN, the server sends a + continuation line, and only then does the client send the data. The server MUST still accept this form.

For the EXTERNAL mechanism, an empty initial response is sent as A01 AUTHENTICATE EXTERNAL =. The long form sends AUTHENTICATE EXTERNAL, receives +, and answers with an empty line.
sections.eli5: With the shortcut you hand over your answer right away. Without it you wait for the "go ahead" sign and then answer.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The extension is subject to many of the security considerations in RFC 3501 and RFC 4422. Servers MUST treat an AUTHENTICATE without an initial response exactly as RFC 3501 defines it.

RFC 3501 has no express line length limit, but some implementations enforce one. Adding the initial response may raise the longest line an IMAP parser must expect, and servers MUST be able to receive the largest initial client response their supported mechanisms might send.

IANA added SASL-IR to the IMAP4 Capabilities Registry.
sections.eli5: The only new thing to watch for is that the request line can now get longer, so the server needs to be ready for a long line.
